scores.accuracy_concern: Schedule 5 preparations (co-codamol, dihydrocodeine, low-strength oral morphine solution) can be supplied in an emergency, so 'most strong painkillers' must be precise; Scottish and English urgent-supply schemes still follow the controlled drug restriction but should be checked; legislation and MHRA pages may not be openable here.
scores.sharpen: Verify the Schedule 5 exceptions and the four-nation position, and close with a concrete step: note the run-out date when the prescription or discharge supply is given.

scores.accuracy_concern: A sequence symmetry ratio of 1.23 shows a modest excess at population level and does not show that any one person's swelling is drug-caused; ankle swelling has many causes (heart failure, amlodipine, venous disease) that still need assessment; the Read 2021 lead is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Keep the sequence ratio out of the public caption, say 'some' rather than 'often', and add what the prescriber might do instead (lower the dose, stop, or look for another cause).

scores.accuracy_concern: Strengths (10 mg in 5 ml and 100 mg in 5 ml, a tenfold difference) must be verified from the BNF or SPC; NPSA RRR05 (2008) covers opioid dosing errors generally and may be archived, so a published paper on concentrate errors would strengthen the claim.
scores.sharpen: Put the verified 'ten times' in the headline and give families one question to ask at every new bottle: which strength is this?

scores.accuracy_concern: Lumbar spinal stenosis and peripheral arterial disease often coexist in older people, so the history points towards a cause but does not exclude the other; pulses or ankle brachial pressure still need checking; likelihood ratios must not be turned into 'times more likely'.
scores.sharpen: Add that circulation problems and stenosis often coexist, so pulses are still checked, and keep the likelihood ratios as 'strong pointers' in plain words.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Unfavourable long-term pain outcome' was defined differently across studies; the about 1 in 5 figure is for knee in the best-quality studies; the post must also say most people get substantial relief so it does not discourage surgery that would help.
scores.sharpen: Pair the 1 in 5 with the fact that most people get good relief, and give the two questions to ask the surgeon.

scores.accuracy_concern: Craig 2012 studied all adults admitted with severe paracetamol liver injury, not older people, and 'older' there is relative within that series; the post must not imply that double-dosing in older people commonly causes liver failure; the BNF caution for adults under 50 kg needs exact wording.
scores.sharpen: State that the Scottish series was of adults of all ages, and add the low body weight caution that applies to many frail older people.

scores.values_concern: The subject sits close to end-of-life decision debates; the post must stay on symptom relief and must not mention or imply any position on assisted dying or on hastening death.
scores.accuracy_concern: The evidence is observational; 'studies have not found that doses adjusted to symptoms shorten life' is supportable, 'morphine does not shorten life' is not; Thorns 2000 and Portenoy 2006 details are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Keep 'studies have not found' wording, and give families the exact question to ask the nurse when they think a dose is needed; coordinate with C19-19.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Cochrane figures (28% fewer cramps, 10% lower intensity) are relative and need absolute numbers; the stretching claim rests on one small trial (Hallegraeff 2012) and a Cochrane review of non-drug treatments for cramps found the evidence insufficient; the MHRA 2010 advice may not be openable here, so a published source repeating it is needed.
scores.sharpen: Give the quinine effect as absolute numbers of cramps over two weeks, and present stretching as a low-risk thing to try rather than a proven treatment.

scores.accuracy_concern: The findings apply to knee and hip OA only and must not be read as 'paracetamol does not work' for acute pain or fractures; abnormal liver tests were more common with paracetamol but of uncertain importance, so no liver-harm claim should be made.
scores.sharpen: Keep the scope in the first line (knee and hip arthritis), show the 3-point gain against the 9-point noticeable change on one drawn scale, and coordinate with C10-01, which uses the same review.

scores.accuracy_concern: PRECISE enrolled adults with a mean age in the mid-50s, so the application to older people rests on side-effect profiles and should be stated; the NICE NG59 recommendation covers sciatica, not all neuropathic pain.
scores.sharpen: State the trial participants' ages and add what to offer instead for sciatica; space it from C10-06.

scores.accuracy_concern: Bedson and Croft give very wide ranges that depend on definitions, and severe radiographic change does relate to pain on average; the post should say the X-ray is a poor guide, not no guide, and imaging still has a role in atypical cases and surgical planning.
scores.sharpen: Add one line on when imaging does help (unusual features, planning surgery), and give the person a question to ask instead of 'what does the X-ray show?'.

scores.accuracy_concern: Chen 2018 studied surgical patients with a mean age of 52, so the extension to older medical inpatients is judgement; zero as-required doses in hospital does not rule out need at home when activity increases.
scores.sharpen: State the surgical, mean-age-52 population in the caption, and present 'none used' as a prompt to ask about pain at home rather than an automatic no.

scores.accuracy_concern: The hyponatraemia hazard ratio has a wide interval (1.08 to 3.86) from few events, so give the absolute rates (4.6 vs 1.9 per 10,000 person-months) alongside 'about twice'; the hypoglycaemia paper is a nested case-control study with a different design and effect size and is marked unsure.
scores.sharpen: Give absolute rates beside the relative one, and turn the footer into a concrete pre-prescribing check: antidepressant list, sodium, seizure history.

scores.accuracy_concern: The trial compared CBT-I with education, not with sleeping tablets, so 'rather than a sedative' is judgement and must be marked as such; the same trial is used by C11-09.
scores.sharpen: Coordinate with C11-09 so only one post uses McCurry 2021, and mark the sedative comparison as judgement or remove it.

scores.accuracy_concern: Oxycodone also accumulates in renal impairment, so the alternatives named should be limited to those the cited guidance supports (fentanyl, alfentanil, with advice); King 2011 PMID is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Open with the observable sign (new twitching or drowsiness a few days into morphine) rather than the pharmacology, and keep the eGFR caveat for people with little muscle.

scores.accuracy_concern: Most evidence on movement-evoked pain comes from postsurgical trials in adults of all ages; the claim that it relates more closely to function should cite Corbett 2019 or Srikandarajah 2011 specifically; the ANZCA reference is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Give a concrete recording example (a 'pain on standing' line beside 'pain at rest') and link it to the therapy session the person is about to have.

scores.accuracy_concern: Both odds ratios sit close to 1 (loneliness 1.15, CI 1.01 to 1.31; isolation 0.87, CI 0.75 to 0.99), the analysis is cross-sectional, and mean age was 65.8 with participants from age 50, so the 'lonely but less isolated' paradox is fragile and must not be stated as pain making people lonely.
scores.sharpen: Describe the finding as a modest link from one survey and lead with the practical question ('Do you feel lonely?') rather than the paradox.

scores.accuracy_concern: The cost comparison comes from one trial of 64 people (Jessep 2009); Hurley 2007 details and the hip version's evidence are unverified; the effect on pain was smaller than on function.
scores.sharpen: Lead with what happens in a session and the verified 12 sessions over 6 weeks, and present the cost result as from one small trial.

scores.accuracy_concern: Leveille 2009 is observational; the adjusted rate ratio of 1.53 compares multisite pain with no pain, not with single-site pain, so the multisite versus single-site contrast should be given only as the age-adjusted rates (1.18 vs 0.90 per person-year); there is no evidence that recording all sites reduces falls.
scores.sharpen: Report the falls link as rates per person per year with 'linked with', and say what an extra site should change (for example foot pain prompting footwear or podiatry review).

scores.accuracy_concern: Frank 2017 rated the evidence very low quality, so 'more often reported improved pain' must say so plainly; Agnoli 2021 is observational; the SPACE trial excluded most older adults; any tapering rate is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Say in plain words that the studies were small and weak, and keep both sides equal in length: pain often does not worsen with slow reduction, and fast or forced reduction carries real risk.

scores.accuracy_concern: da Costa 2017 pooled adult OA trials and was not an older-adult analysis; Solomon 2010 is observational with confounding by indication, so 'refusing NSAIDs leaves people on opioids with more harm' must stay as a link, not a cause.
scores.sharpen: Lead with a concrete dilemma and drop the gel strand so it does not repeat C10-14, keeping this post on the oral NSAID decision and its checks.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE NG226 places the topical NSAID alongside core treatments (exercise, weight, information), not as a stand-alone first step; the Cochrane NNT is [N to verify]; the 'much less reaches the bloodstream' claim needs the pharmacokinetic source (Kienzler 2010) verified.
scores.sharpen: Replace the NICE opening with a concrete one about the knee and the tube of gel, give the verified number needed to treat in plain words, and coordinate with C10-04 so only one post carries the gel point.

scores.accuracy_concern: Effects were small (standardised mean differences about 0.18) and physical function did not clearly improve; 'group sessions worked best' is a subgroup finding and should be hedged.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the fear ('A referral to psychology does not mean your pain is imagined') and give the size of benefit in plain words.

scores.accuracy_concern: UK eligibility has changed in phases and differs by nation, and official UKHSA and Public Health Scotland pages were not openable here, so the eligibility statement lacks an opened source; 9 in 10 is relative efficacy and needs an absolute figure.
scores.sharpen: Verify current eligibility in each UK nation from an opened source and give the absolute number of cases prevented per 1,000 vaccinated beside '9 in 10'.

scores.accuracy_concern: Fayaz 2016's 62% figure for people 75 and over is a pooled estimate from few age-stratified studies; the under-reporting claim rests on small qualitative work (Gammons and Caswell 2014, unverified).
scores.sharpen: Keep it as a public preparation card and differentiate it from C10-01 and C10-21, which make the goal and function point for clinicians.

scores.values_concern: The post must not imply that prescribers in deprived areas give worse care, or state a policy position; the ethical judgement on fair access should be marked as judgement.
scores.accuracy_concern: Mordecai 2018 is area-level (ecological) data, so 'people with the fewest resources are more often managed with opioids' is an individual-level inference it cannot support; Todd 2018 details are unverified; 'medicines that help least' overstates the evidence.
scores.sharpen: Verify Todd 2018, keep the area-level caveat, and replace 'medicines that help least' with 'limited benefit for long-term pain'.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 'first two days' window is unsupported: constipation and accumulation effects can take longer to appear, and the early-fall-risk studies are observational; the bowel threshold is still [N to verify]; the gabapentinoid respiratory depression warnings (MHRA 2017 and 2019) need exact dates and wording.
scores.sharpen: Drop the two-day frame unless a source supports it, name the medicines in the first line, and give the call-back signs with a verified bowel threshold.

scores.accuracy_concern: A trial average does not show hidden large responders, and a one-person trial is also moved by natural fluctuation and regression to the mean; the post should not imply that a person who feels better on a drug has proved it works. The Opioids Aware wording on trials and the Abdulla 2013 PMID are unverified.
scores.sharpen: Open with a concrete situation (a tablet for knee pain started with no review date) and give the goal, review date and stop rule in the first lines rather than a statement about trial averages.

scores.accuracy_concern: Single US clinic, 600 visits, published 2006; 'no new therapy at that visit' does not equal undertreatment, since some people were already on a suitable plan; applicability to UK wards and care homes now is uncertain.
scores.sharpen: Reframe the finding as 'no documented plan after a high score', state the single-clinic 2006 limits in the post, and add one concrete audit question a ward can use.

scores.accuracy_concern: The pain-monitoring model cited (Thomee 1997) came from young women with patellofemoral pain, not older adults with OA; the NICE NG226 wording on discomfort and the benefit timescale are unverified; the 'settles by next morning' rule needs a source in older adults.
scores.sharpen: Anchor the acceptable-ache rule to a programme or trial in older adults with OA (for example ESCAPE-pain materials) and give a verified timescale, or merge with C10-17.

scores.accuracy_concern: The claim that verbal scales give 'steadier' answers is a reliability claim that Herr 2004 and Closs 2004 may not support as phrased (they mainly report completion and preference); the large-print advice attributed to Schofield 2018 is unverified.
scores.sharpen: Frame it as choosing a scale the person can use and keeping to it, and consider merging with C10-21 into one assessment post.

allocation_reason: Fourteen candidates score 44 or more and 29 of 31 clear about 36 with no disqualifying flag, so the category can fill the maximum with strong, well-sourced ideas; the tail (C10-01, 02, 07, 08, 20) is weaker or overlaps.
balance_note: Top 14 by score: 7 public (12, 06, 30, 09, 25, 03, 16), 3 both (10, 15, 27), 4 practitioners (22, 26, 13, 18), which is a good audience spread. The weakness is topic: 10 of the 14 are about medicines (two gabapentinoid posts, 06 and 26, need spacing), knee and hip arthritis recurs (15, 16, 30), and no 'Care that works' or 'Who gets left out' post makes the top 14. Consider swapping one medicine post (18 or 13) for C10-17 (ESCAPE-pain) or C10-21 (pain on movement) to include a non-drug approach, and pick only one of C10-04 and C10-14 if either is used.
